issues.description: The Problem Statement and Solution expect StockIngredient to have a constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the Template repository's StockIngredient class only provides a constructor with an extra boolean parameter StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). This constructor parameter mismatch will confuse students and prevent them from instantiating StockIngredient with the expected three-argument form (used in examples and in the solution), blocking straightforward implementation and testing.
issues.suggestedFix: Add (or restore) the three-argument constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) to the template StockIngredient class (or overload the existing constructor) so it matches the problem specification and the solution. For example, add a constructor that delegates to the current implementation (e.g., public StockIngredient(String name,int price,int quantity) { this(name, price, quantity, false); }). This preserves any strictValidation behavior while providing the expected API.

issues.description: The problem statement's class diagram specifies a StockIngredient constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the template repository's StockIngredient only provides a constructor StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). The solution repository implements the expected three-argument constructor. This mismatch will confuse students when the exercise instructions and UML show creating StockIngredient objects with three arguments while the provided starter code requires a different constructor signature, potentially causing compile errors or preventing straightforward implementation.
issues.suggestedFix: Provide a three-argument constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) in the template (e.g., overload the existing constructor) so the template matches the UML and the solution. Alternatively, update the problem statement/UML to document the four-argument constructor if that was intentional.
